title: Notice and Email Writing
tagline: The prescribed pair: one situation, two fixed formats, fifty words each.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE English Language syllabus (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by Scribd, Oswal Publishers and Shaalaa; cisce.org returned 403). Every model text, question and answer is original practice; no board examination paper was consulted.

overview.intro: The ICSE Language paper sets notice and email as a pair: one given situation, two short compositions, each normally limited to about fifty words. The pairing is the point of the question — you are tested on whether you can carry the same information into two different addresses, in the two forms the board prescribes, without wasting a word. The notice is for a public board: it names the institution, carries the label NOTICE, dates itself, gives a heading, states what is happening, when, where, who must attend or act and why, and closes with the name and designation of the signer. The email is for one reader: an address in the To field, a subject line that names the purpose, a salutation, the compressed message, a courteous close and your name. This chapter teaches both formats block by block, then the compression skill that the fifty-word limit actually rewards, and finally the errors that cost marks — a missing date, an absent subject line, an inconsistency between the two drafts, or a word limit overrun. Every model and question here is original practice against the registered syllabus.

learn.title: Before you read: what the paired question really asks

blocks.text: Notice and email arrive together in the paper because modern communication tests the same competence twice: can you write the right form for the right reader? The notice speaks to everybody — a school, a club, an office — and must work at a glance from a board in a corridor. The email speaks to one person and must work in an inbox where nobody will read twice. Understanding that difference explains every rule that follows: the notice is labelled and dated because boards are scanned, while the email carries a subject line because inboxes are listed. Examiners mark this question on four things. Format, because a notice without its label and date is not a notice. Completeness, because the situation handed to you contains details that must all appear — what is happening, when, where, who and why. Accuracy, because a date or time altered from the question is a lost mark. And economy, because the word limit is part of the instruction, and a draft that overruns has failed the task however good its English. Prepare therefore to learn two skeletons by heart and to practise squeezing real situations into them until the compression is automatic.

items: The notice addresses a corridor; the email addresses an inbox.
Format, completeness, accuracy and economy are what the marks reward.
Every detail in the given situation must appear somewhere in both drafts.
The word limit is an instruction, not a suggestion.
Two skeletons learned well turn the question into routine.

blocks.text: A notice is a small box of fixed parts, and each part has a job. At the top goes the name of the institution issuing it — the school, the club, the office — because a notice without an issuer has no authority. Directly beneath comes the word NOTICE, in capitals or prominent lettering, which tells a reader in half a second what this document is. Then the date of issue: notices are perishable, and a reader must know how fresh the information is. Next comes the heading — a short title naming the event or matter, written to be read from a distance. The body follows, and it is written in telegraphic but grammatical sentences carrying the five Ws: what is to happen, when it will happen (date and time), where it will happen (venue), who it is for or who must act, and why it is being called. The closing block gives the name of the signer and the designation — the head prefect, the secretary, the class teacher — because accountability attaches to a signature rather than to a box. Everything is kept inside the word limit, and nothing decorative survives: a notice is a container for facts, and the craft lies in never dropping one.

blocks.text: An email keeps the etiquette of a letter inside the economy of a memo. The To field takes the recipient’s address exactly as the question gives it — a mistyped or invented address is an accuracy mark thrown away. The Subject line is the notice’s heading in another form: one line naming the purpose, so the recipient knows before opening what the message concerns. The salutation follows the relationship — a teacher or principal receives a courteous greeting, a committee a formal one, a peer a plain one — and the register stays consistent with it. The body then carries the same five Ws as the notice, in connected sentences rather than telegraphic fragments, because an email is read by one person who expects a message rather than a list. The close is courteous and proportionate: a complimentary close, then the sender’s name, and where the situation gives one, the designation. Two habits separate strong answers from weak ones. The subject line is never blank and never vague — “Excursion” scores; “Hello” does not. And the tone never contradicts the recipient: the same event announced to a school noticeboard and to a parent by email should feel like two different pieces of writing from one careful writer.

items: To: the exact address given in the question — no invention, no abbreviation.
Subject: one line that names the purpose, never blank, never vague.
Salutation and close: matched to the relationship and kept consistent.
Body: the five Ws in connected sentences, not telegraphic fragments.
Register: formal where the recipient requires it, throughout.

learn.title: The fifty-word craft: compressing the situation

blocks.text: The word limit is where this question is actually won. Fifty words include every block — the heading, the date, the signature — so the body has roughly thirty in which to carry five facts. The technique is subtraction with a rule: keep what the reader must act on, remove what the reader may assume. Greetings and pleasantries shrink to the prescribed minimum; articles and connectives tighten; repetition between heading and body disappears — if the heading says EXCURSION TO THE HILL STATION, the body need not say again that there will be an excursion. What may never be cut: dates, times, venues, the names of those who must act, and the reason where the reason is the point of the notice. A useful practice is to list the question’s details as five or six fragments first — the skeleton — then write the draft around them and count. If you are over, cut adjectives before facts; if you are under, you have probably dropped a W, so check again. The companion rule concerns the pair: because both drafts come from one situation, each must be complete in itself — a reader of only the notice, and a reader of only the email, must each know everything they need.

learn.title: Common errors, and how to avoid them

blocks.text: The marks lost in this question are rarely about English; they are about procedure. The notice omits the date of issue, or the label NOTICE, or the signer’s designation — each is a mark sitting on the floor. The heading is missing or so long that the body has no room. The email has no subject line, or the subject line says something general like “About the trip”, which tells the recipient nothing they did not already know. Details drift from the question: the date given in the box is changed, the venue is invented, or the time is written in the wrong format — the examiner marks against the question paper and rewards fidelity exactly. The two drafts contradict each other — the notice says Friday while the email says Saturday — which loses marks in both halves at once. And the word limit is overrun because the writer trusted the count at the end instead of counting while drafting. The defence against all of these is mechanical: build from a detail list, write inside the skeleton, count as you finish each draft, and read once against the question’s box of facts. Procedure, in this question, is the skill.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: The examinable core of this chapter is recall under time pressure. Learn the notice skeleton — issuer, label, date, heading, five-W body, signature with designation — and the email skeleton — To, subject, salutation, five-W body, close, name — until you can write them without thinking. Then practise the pairing: take one situation and produce both drafts, checking that each is complete alone and consistent with the other. In the examination, read the given situation twice and lift every fact into a list before writing; the facts are the marks. The questions below drill the format, the compression and the diagnosis of faulty drafts — attempt them under a ten-minute limit for the pair, which is the pace the paper demands. This page’s models are original practice written against the registered syllabus rather than board papers; where your school prescribes a particular variant of the notice or email form, that variant governs, and the principles of completeness and economy here apply to it equally.

items: Learn both skeletons to automatic recall.
Lift every fact from the question into a list before drafting.
Each draft must be complete alone and consistent with the other.
Practise the pair under a ten-minute limit.
Your school’s prescribed format variant governs; the principles do not change.

questions.prompt: Which block comes immediately after the institution name in a school notice?
options: The word NOTICE and the date of issue
questions.answer: The word NOTICE and the date of issue
questions.explanation: The notice opens with the issuer, then labels itself NOTICE and dates itself, before the heading and the body follow.
questions.commonMistake: Salutation and subject line belong to the email, not the notice.

questions.prompt: The subject line of an email should:
options: Name the purpose of the message in one clear line
Repeat the institution’s name in full
State the word count of the message
questions.answer: Name the purpose of the message in one clear line
questions.explanation: The subject is the email’s heading: it lets the recipient know before opening what the message concerns, so it must name the purpose rather than greet.
questions.commonMistake: A greeting in the subject line wastes the one line the format gives you for purpose.

questions.prompt: Every detail in a given situation must appear in:
options: Both drafts, each complete on its own
The notice only, since it is public
The email only, since it is direct
Whichever draft you write more confidently
questions.answer: Both drafts, each complete on its own
questions.explanation: The two drafts have different readers, and a reader of only one of them must still know everything needed to act.
questions.commonMistake: Splitting the facts between the drafts leaves each one incomplete.

questions.prompt: A notice whose heading already names the event should in its body:
options: Give the remaining facts without repeating the heading’s words
Repeat the heading in the first sentence
Add a second heading for the date
Begin with a greeting to the students
questions.answer: Give the remaining facts without repeating the heading’s words
questions.explanation: Economy under the fifty-word limit means cutting what the reader has already read — repetition of the heading is the first thing to go.
questions.commonMistake: Repetition feels emphatic but spends words that a required W needs.

questions.prompt: The five facts every notice body must carry are what, when, where, who and ______.
questions.explanation: The five Ws are the completeness rule for both drafts: each must let its reader know the reason where the reason matters.
questions.commonMistake: Do not substitute “how” — the registered set ends with why.

questions.prompt: State four blocks that a school notice must contain.
questions.answer: The name of the institution issuing the notice; the label NOTICE; the date of issue; a heading naming the matter; the body carrying what, when, where, who and why; and the closing signature with the signer’s name and designation. Any four of these six complete the answer.
questions.explanation: Four distinct blocks are named from the prescribed skeleton, which is what a two-mark recall expects.
questions.commonMistake: Do not include email blocks — salutation and To address do not belong to a notice.

questions.prompt: Your draft notice has run to seventy words. How do you bring it within the limit without losing a mark?
questions.answer: Cut in a fixed order. First remove anything the heading has already said, since repetition of the event is the commonest waste. Second tighten ornaments — adjectives, articles, connectives — while keeping every fact. Third merge sentences that repeat the same W, so date and venue stand together. Facts are never cut: dates, times, venue, who must act and why are the marked content. Then recount against the limit printed on the paper, because the count itself is part of the instruction.
questions.explanation: The answer gives an ordered subtraction plan that protects the facts and ends with the recount.
questions.commonMistake: Cutting a date or the venue to save words loses more marks than the overrun did.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of each block of an email and what an examiner looks for in it.
questions.answer: The To field identifies the single reader; an examiner checks that the address is exactly the one the question provides, since invention or abbreviation is an accuracy loss. The Subject line names the purpose in one line, so the message can be found and sorted; a blank or vague subject shows that the writer has not understood the block’s function. The salutation establishes the relationship, and its courtesy must match the recipient — a principal, a teacher and a peer each require a different degree of formality, and the register must then be kept consistent through the body. The body carries what, when, where, who and why in connected sentences, because unlike a notice an email is read by one person who expects a message rather than a list; every fact from the given situation must appear here or in the salutation-free blocks around it. The complimentary close and the sender’s name complete the etiquette, signalling who is answerable for the message. Across all blocks the examiner weighs economy: the whole draft must sit inside the word limit, so each block must be present but brief — completeness in the smallest number of words the instruction allows.
questions.explanation: Each block is named with its function and the specific mark an examiner attaches to it, closing on economy as the shared constraint.
questions.commonMistake: Do not merely list the blocks; the question asks what each is for and what is looked for.

questions.prompt: A notice and an email are drafted on the same situation. What makes each complete, and how should they differ?
questions.answer: Completeness is judged reader by reader. The notice is complete when a person passing the board knows what is happening, when and where it will happen, who must attend or act, why it has been called, which body has issued the information, on what date, and who is answerable for it — every W plus issuer, label and signature. The email is complete when its single recipient knows the same essentials from the To line through the close, with the purpose carried in the subject line. Neither may borrow from the other: a notice is telegraphic and labelled because boards are scanned at a glance; an email is connected and courteous because one person opens it expecting a message. Their differences, then, are of address and register rather than of content — the notice speaks with the institution’s voice to everybody, the email with the writer’s voice to somebody. What they share is discipline: each stays inside its word limit, each is accurate to the question’s facts, and each is consistent with its pair so that no reader of one is told a different date from the reader of the other.
questions.explanation: The answer defines completeness per reader, contrasts address and register, and joins them on the shared discipline of limit, accuracy and consistency.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer as if the two drafts were one answer split in half; each stands alone.

questions.prompt: “In this question, procedure scores more than style.” Discuss, with reference to what examiners reward.
questions.answer: The proposition is close to true, and the reason is structural. Notice and email are format questions: the mark scheme is visibly attached to blocks — issuer, label, date, heading, body, signature; To, subject, salutation, body, close — and a beautifully written draft missing the label NOTICE or the date of issue cannot recover those marks, because the marks belong to the block and not to the prose. Completeness is similarly procedural: the question hands over a box of facts, and the examiner matches the draft against it item by item, so a writer who lifts the facts into a list before writing will pass this stage almost mechanically while a stylish writer who trusts memory may drop the venue. Accuracy of detail is pure procedure — a changed date is marked wrong however elegant the sentence. Economy too: the word limit is an instruction, and only the habit of counting during composition guarantees it. Style is not irrelevant — grammar, register and the fit between tone and recipient are all rewarded — but style is the second-order mark here; it decorates a draft that has already been scored on its structure. The counter-case deserves stating: two candidates with identical formats will be separated by sentence quality, so style decides the higher band. Yet that is precisely the point — procedure qualifies you for the band, and style then places you within it. Learn the skeletons first, and the writing has something to be good inside.
questions.explanation: The essay grounds every procedural mark in the mark scheme’s structure, concedes that style separates candidates within the band, and turns the concession into the ordering of preparation.
questions.commonMistake: Do not dismiss style altogether; the discuss form wants the counter-case and the ordering it implies.
